title: Two Patient Deaths Put Tustin Oral Surgeon’s License and Anesthesia Permit on the Line
html:
A 77-year-old implant patient stopped breathing about 30 minutes into her procedure, and emergency services weren’t called for roughly another hour, the Dental Board of California alleges. She never regained consciousness.

The board is seeking to revoke or suspend the license and general anesthesia permit of Dr. Craig C. Thiede, an oral and maxillofacial surgeon in Tustin, over his care of that patient and a second patient who died in 2025, according to a first amended accusation filed Oct. 15. The board first filed an accusation against him in August 2025.

The woman, who had high blood pressure and diabetes, came in on Nov. 3, 2022, to have her remaining upper teeth extracted, implants placed, and a prosthesis delivered under sedation. Thiede classified her as ASA II. When she stopped breathing, she didn’t respond to stimuli despite manual ventilation and reversal medication, according to the accusation. She suffered an anoxic brain injury and later died.

Her consent forms weren’t signed by her or Thiede, the board alleges, and her records lacked intraoperative vitals, the anesthesia infusion rate and stop time, the amount of remifentanil used, and an ECG strip covering the full procedure. The board also alleges he didn’t obtain a medical consultation before treating her and didn’t report the event within the seven days state law requires. His report to the board was submitted Nov. 14, 2022.

The second patient came in on June 17, 2025, for a single extraction. His chart listed a pacemaker, heart stents, a history of bypass surgery, congestive heart conditions, kidney disease, and insulin-dependent diabetes, and Thiede classified him as ASA III. His records don’t indicate the procedure was a dental emergency, the board notes.

Monitors and anesthesia both started recording at 10:29 a.m., and the chart lists a surgical end time of 10:32 a.m., according to the accusation. The office called emergency services at about 10:44 a.m. The patient went into cardiac arrest during transport and was pronounced dead at the hospital at 11:27 a.m.

In the second case, the board alleges gross negligence for failing to consider the patient’s high-risk conditions before providing deep sedation and general anesthesia in an office setting, and for records that don’t show monitoring before anesthesia began.

The allegations haven’t been proven. Thiede’s license and general anesthesia permit remain active while the case is pending before California’s Office of Administrative Hearings, and no response from him has been reported.

In the first case, the board’s gross negligence allegation rests on documentation: what it says Thiede’s records failed to show before, during, and after the procedure. Across both cases, the allegations center on patient selection, monitoring, and recordkeeping rather than on who else was in the room, and both patients’ charts listed chronic medical conditions before anyone was sedated.

That makes it a counterpoint to a Florida death Dentaltown covered recently. In that case, a father of five died after a full-mouth implant procedure under IV sedation, and his family is pushing for a law requiring a separately licensed anesthesia provider in the room. His wife has also questioned whether he was an appropriate candidate for sedation in the first place.

When a medically complex patient wants to be sedated in your office, what makes you bring in a separate anesthesia provider, get a medical consult, or send the case to a hospital instead?

Sources:
